Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the first page of an onboarding document for a new backend engineer joining a payments team. Around 200 words.

# Welcome to the payments team

You're joining the team that moves money for every customer transaction. Read this page first, then the runbook links at the bottom before you touch production.

## What we own

We run authorization, capture, settlement, and refunds for the checkout flow. `ledger` records every state change to a transaction. `gateway` talks to card processors and banks. `reconciler` compares our records against processor reports nightly and flags mismatches.

## How we work

Every change to `ledger` or `gateway` requires a second engineer's review before merge, no exceptions. We deploy `gateway` on Tuesdays and Thursdays only, after the reconciler's nightly run confirms the previous day balanced. Idan Reyes owns the on-call rotation. Check PagerDuty for the current schedule.

## Money is not like other data

A bug in a recommendation engine loses engagement. A bug here loses money, and sometimes we cannot get it back.

Treat every write to `ledger` as irreversible until proven otherwise.

Write the test that proves the amount is right before you write the code that moves it.

## First week

Set up your local environment with `make payments-dev`, then shadow one on-call rotation before you carry the pager yourself. After that, work through the incident postmortems in `docs/incidents/` — five years of mistakes we made once and don't repeat.

Add a section on who to ask for what.

For questions about `ledger` schema or transaction states, ask Priya Shah. She wrote the current model and the migration history in `docs/ledger/`.

Processor integration issues go to Marcus Webb, covering declined authorizations, gateway timeouts, and certificate rotations. He owns the relationships with our card processor contacts and can tell you whether a failure is our bug or their outage.

For reconciliation mismatches, ask whoever ran the previous night's on-call shift first, and check the incident channel history before escalating. Most mismatches repeat a known pattern, so someone has likely already diagnosed the one you're looking at.

File access requests, covering the production database, PagerDuty, and the processor dashboards, go in the `payments-access` queue. Idan Reyes approves these but does not grant them directly, and provisioning takes up to one business day.

If a question doesn't fit these categories, ask in `#payments-eng`. Someone there will point you to the right person or tell you it's in the docs.
